questions.prompt: Mean latency is 20 ms but P99 is 95 ms. A user complains about occasional stalls. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: A rare slow path exists; investigate the tail (retries, GC, cache misses)
P99 is an arithmetic error, because it exceeds the mean latency value
The system is uniformly slow, so optimise the average code path first
Throughput must be exactly 1/0.02 requests per second in this system
questions.explanation: The tail is much longer than the mean, which indicates rare slow events rather than uniform slowness.
Rank = ceil(0.95*20)=19, the 19th sorted value is 30.

questions.prompt: A pipeline of 3 serial stages takes 6 ms, 14 ms and 20 ms per item. What is the maximum throughput in items per second if one worker runs the stages back to back?
questions.explanation: Total 40 ms per item, so 1/0.04 = 25 items/s.

questions.prompt: A data loader must keep 50 batches/s flowing while each batch takes 200 ms to arrive from disk. How many batches must be in flight on average (Little's law)?
A job reports cpu_s = 7.5 and wall_s = 2.5 on a machine with 4 cores. What is the CPU utilization as a fraction of all 4 cores (0 to 1)?
Why should interval timing use time.perf_counter() rather than time.time()?
options: time.time() is not available in Python 3, so it cannot be used to time
perf_counter reports CPU time only, which is what latency measures here
perf_counter is monotonic and high-resolution; time.time() can jump if the clock is set
time.time() only has whole-second resolution on all systems, which is too coarse
questions.explanation: perf_counter is a monotonic clock designed for intervals.

questions.prompt: A function is timed once, takes 40 ms, and the new version takes 36 ms on one run. What is the best next step?
options: Run the new version only, since the old one is already well known
Ship it: it is 10% faster, which is a clear gain on this function
Take the maximum of the two runs instead, as the safe worst case
Repeat both many times, alternating, and compare medians to the spread
questions.explanation: One run per version cannot separate a 10% effect from timing noise.

questions.prompt: 30% of a program's time is a stage you can speed up 3x; the rest cannot change. What is the overall speedup (two decimals)?
A list of 2,000,000 distinct Python floats costs about 8 bytes of pointer plus 24 bytes per float object. Estimate its size in MB (1 MB = 10^6 bytes).
Which statement about tracemalloc versus RSS is correct?
options: RSS counts only the memory that was freed, while tracemalloc counts the rest
tracemalloc peak equals the RSS exactly, as both count the same memory
tracemalloc measures GPU memory, while the RSS measures the host memory
RSS includes the interpreter and libraries, so exceeds the traced Python allocations
questions.explanation: RSS is an OS number covering the whole process; tracemalloc counts Python allocations.

questions.prompt: Your camera node must run at 30 Hz. Which latency statistics do you report and what do you do if P99 is 41 ms?
rubric: Computes the budget 1/30 s = 33.3 ms and reports median, P99 and maximum with sample count.
Concludes P99 = 41 ms misses the deadline in about 1% of frames.
Proposes a measurement-led next step (profile the slow frames, check queueing, GC, or I/O waits) rather than guessing.

questions.prompt: A teammate says the pipeline is 'CPU bound' because htop shows it busy. What additional measurements would confirm or reject that?

remediationRefs.label: Review: Wall time versus CPU time

rubric: Compares CPU time with wall time over the same window (utilization near 1 per core).
Checks other resources with USE: disk, network, memory saturation, lock waits.
Names a falsifiable test, such as removing the compute stage and seeing whether wall time barely changes.
